findings.evidence: "Check the message again and enter all six."
findings.fix: Name the source explicitly, e.g. "Check the text message you received and enter all six digits."
findings.location: Two-factor setup, verification code - first message block ("5 digits" message)
findings.violation: "The message" is ambiguous - it could mean the SMS/email containing the code or this error message itself, so the instruction doesn't clearly tell the user where to look.

findings.location: Two-factor setup, verification code - first message block
findings.violation: "all six" has no noun, leaving it unclear whether the user should enter six digits, characters, or something else.

findings.evidence: Predictable mistake: yes / Suggested fix: none
findings.fix: Propose a preventive fix, such as disabling submission until 6 digits are entered or showing a live digit count.
findings.location: Two-factor setup, verification code - first message block (fields)
findings.violation: Calling a mistake "predictable" implies it can be prevented, yet no preventive fix is proposed (e.g. a live digit counter or disabling submit until six digits are entered), so the review only reacts to the error instead of preventing it.

findings.fix: Delay the on-blur check with a short debounce so late-arriving autofill digits are included before validating.
findings.location: Two-factor setup, verification code - first message block (fields)
findings.violation: Firing the length check on blur risks a false positive during autofill, since many OTP autofill flows populate digits one at a time and can trigger blur before all six have landed, showing "5 digits" while entry is still in progress.

findings.evidence: "which stops an intercepted code from being reused later"
findings.fix: Cut the rationale and keep the actionable sentence, e.g. "This verification code has expired. Request a new code and enter it here."
findings.location: Two-factor setup, verification code - second message block (expired code)
findings.violation: This clause explains security rationale instead of telling the user what to do, adds length, and implies the user's specific code may have been intercepted, which can alarm them unnecessarily.

findings.evidence: "selectable, offers a resend code button in place of the message"
findings.fix: Rewrite as distinct clauses, e.g. "Replace the message with a 'Resend code' button," and either explain what "selectable" refers to or remove it if it's a leftover from another row.
findings.location: Two-factor setup, verification code - second message block, Suggested fix field
findings.violation: The text is not a grammatical sentence and conflates two unrelated ideas ("selectable" and a resend button) with no clear subject, so it can't be acted on as written.

findings.fix: Clear the field (at least once a new code is requested) instead of preserving the expired value.
findings.location: Two-factor setup, verification code - second message block, Input on resubmission field
findings.violation: Preserving the entered code makes no sense once it's known to be expired - the value is guaranteed invalid, and leaving it risks the user resubmitting the same expired code after requesting a new one.

findings.fix: Include the year, e.g. "This promo code ended on 30 June 2026."
findings.location: Billing, promo code - first message block (code ended)
findings.violation: The date omits the year, making it ambiguous which 30 June is meant, especially for codes that could span a year boundary.

findings.fix: Reclassify as a predictable mistake, or add a note explaining why expired promo codes are treated as unpredictable here.
findings.location: Billing, promo code - first message block (fields)
findings.violation: Expired promo codes (e.g. from an old marketing email) are a common, foreseeable occurrence, unlike the precise 10-minute 2FA expiry documented elsewhere, so classifying this as unpredictable is inconsistent with the reasoning used for similar cases.

findings.evidence: Both rows are marked "Predictable mistake: no," but one is "Fires: on-submit" and the other "Fires: on-blur."
findings.fix: Apply one consistent rule for Fires timing based on predictability, or document why the expired-code and expired-promo-code cases differ.
findings.location: Billing, promo code - first message block vs. Two-factor setup - second message block
findings.violation: The two "unpredictable mistake" cases use different trigger timing with no stated reason, while the two "predictable mistake" cases are consistently on-blur, suggesting the Fires rule isn't actually tied to predictability or one of the two values is wrong.

findings.evidence: Predictable mistake: yes / Suggested fix: none
findings.fix: Propose a preventive fix, such as disabling incompatible promo codes for the selected plan or surfacing the plan requirement before the user applies the code.
findings.location: Billing, promo code - second message block (fields)
findings.violation: As with the 2FA length-mismatch row, marking this predictable implies it's preventable, yet no preventive fix is proposed (e.g. filtering out annual-only codes when a monthly plan is selected).

findings.evidence: Signal: bold text set larger than the field label, icon (identical in every row)
findings.fix: Scale the signal to severity, e.g. a lighter signal (no icon) for simple format errors like the digit-count mismatch, reserving bold text plus icon for expired-code or security-relevant errors.
findings.location: Signal field, all four message blocks
findings.violation: Every message - from a minor, easily-fixed digit miscount to an expired security code - gets the same visually loud treatment, so severity isn't communicated and repeated low-stakes errors risk desensitizing users to the strongest signal.
